question: Two busway tie sections are fed from separate sources. ATS 7.4 requires a phasing test, and it must be done:
choices: From a temporary generator before the permanent sources are connected
From the permanent sources that will feed them
With a phase-rotation meter on de-energized bus
Only if the busway is rated above 1000 V
explanation: The purpose is to prove the real sources line up in phase across the tie. A temporary source can't prove that, so ATS says the test must come from the permanent sources. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.4.B.5 and D.5.

question: A 4.76 kV nonsegregated-phase bus run gets a field withstand test, and the manufacturer is silent. The maximum ac value in ATS Table 100.17 is:
choices: 20 kV
explanation: Table 100.17 gives 14.2 kV ac for 4.76 kV nonsegregated bus. 27.0 kV is the 8.25 kV and 15.0 kV row. That table has no dc value for this class, and ATS says to use the ac value where no dc value is shown. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.4.B.3 and Table 100.17.

question: How is the dielectric withstand applied to a metal-enclosed busway under ATS 7.4?
choices: All three phases tied together and tested to ground in one shot
Phase-to-phase only, with ground floating
Phase-to-neutral, with the enclosure isolated
Phase-to-ground, with the phases not under test grounded
explanation: Each phase is tested to ground with the other phases grounded. Values come from the manufacturer or Table 100.17. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.4.B.3.

question: On outdoor rigid bus rated 34.5 kV (nominal), the manufacturer gives no withstand value. ATS 7.21 uses Table 100.19, which gives a maximum ac test of:
explanation: Table 100.19 lists 42.0 kV ac and 59.4 kV dc for the 34.5 kV class, applied for one minute. 30.0 kV is the 25 kV class and 57.0 kV is the 46 kV class. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.21.B.3 and Table 100.19.

question: Which inspection item is specific to outdoor bus structures in ATS 7.21?
choices: Support insulators are clean and undamaged
Weep-hole plugs are installed per the manufacturer
Busway joint shields are in place
Space heaters are energized
explanation: Outdoor bus is carried on station post insulators, so ATS checks that they are clean and intact. Weep-hole plugs, joint shields, and heaters belong to metal-enclosed busway under ATS 7.4. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.21.A.4.

question: How does ATS 7.21 set up the insulation-resistance test on outdoor bus rated below 46 kV?
choices: All phases tied together and measured to ground in one reading
Phase-to-phase only, with ground lifted
Each phase to ground, with the other phases grounded
Across each support insulator individually
explanation: Each bus phase is measured to ground with the other phases grounded. The voltage comes from the manufacturer or Table 100.1. The step is written for equipment rated below 46 kV. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.21.B.2.

question: A 350 ft low-voltage busway run reads 0.25 MΩ phase-to-ground, and the manufacturer gives no minimum. Under ATS 7.4:
choices: Accept, because 0.25 MΩ exceeds 100 kΩ
Investigate; the minimum is about 0.29 MΩ
Accept, because long runs have no minimum
Proceed to the withstand test to see whether the insulation holds
explanation: Minimum MΩ = 100 / length in feet = 100 / 350 = 0.286 MΩ. The reading is below that, so investigate. ATS says not to proceed with the dielectric withstand until insulation resistance is raised above minimum. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.4.D.2.a.

question: A 69 kV outdoor bus structure is being accepted with no manufacturer data. Which statement matches ATS 7.21?
choices: Insulation resistance at 5 kV is required first, then a 160 kV ac withstand for 1 minute
Withstand up to 84 kV ac for 1 minute; the IR step covers only below 46 kV
No dielectric test applies above 46 kV
Withstand at 118.8 kV ac for 15 minutes
explanation: Table 100.19 gives 84.0 kV ac (118.8 kV dc) for the 69 kV class, for one minute. The 7.21 insulation-resistance step names equipment below 46 kV. Power factor is optional. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.21.B.2, B.3, B.4 and Table 100.19.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.21.B.2, B.3, B.4 and Table 100.19

question: You have only a dc hipot, and Table 100.17 shows no dc value for 15 kV nonsegregated bus. ATS 7.4 says:
choices: Use 1.414 times the ac value as dc
Skip the withstand and rely on megger readings
Use the 37.5 kV dc value borrowed from the switchgear table, Table 100.2
Use the ac value, so the withstand is done at 27 kV ac
explanation: Where Table 100.17 shows no dc value, ATS says an ac value is to be used. Its note also says the dc column, where it exists, doesn't create a requirement for dc testing. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.4.B.3 and Table 100.17 note 2.

question: Identify the device in the photo. It hooks onto a run of overhead busway at an opening in the bus housing and has its own ON/OFF handle.
choices: Busway plug-in unit (bus plug)
Busway expansion fitting
Feeder busway end closure
Cable tap box with no disconnect
explanation: A plug-in unit, often called a bus plug, stabs onto the busway bars at a plug-in opening and feeds a branch circuit through its own fused switch or breaker, so it has an operating handle. An expansion fitting or end closure is part of the bus run itself and has no handle. Square D lists the PQ3606G as a fusible plug-in unit for I-Line busway, with a mounting hook that lines up with the opening. Feeder busway has no plug-in openings, so bus plugs only go on plug-in style runs.
reference: Manufacturer product page: Schneider Electric (Square D) PQ3606G and I-Line busway range page, se.com; per manufacturer data
image_alt: Gray steel box with a large ON/OFF label, warning labels and an operating handle on the right side.

question: You take an access cover off a medium-voltage bus run. All three phase bars share one housing, with grounded metal barriers between them. This is:
choices: Nonsegregated-phase bus
Segregated-phase bus
Isolated-phase bus
Cable bus
explanation: Segregated-phase bus has all phases in a common metal enclosure with metal barriers between phases. Nonsegregated-phase bus is the same common enclosure with no barriers. Isolated-phase bus gives each phase its own metal housing with an air space to the next. Cable bus uses insulated cables as the phase conductors. These are separate rows when you look up withstand values, so identify the type before you pick a number. Source: IEEE C37.23-2015, clause 3 (types of metal-enclosed bus assemblies).
reference: IEEE C37.23-2015, clause 3 (types of metal-enclosed bus assemblies)

question: Which description fits isolated-phase bus?
choices: All three phases in one enclosure with no barriers
All three phases in one enclosure with metal barriers between them
Each phase conductor in its own metal housing, separated from the next housing by air
Insulated cables in a common enclosure with no barriers
explanation: Isolated-phase bus encloses each phase conductor in its own metal housing, with an air gap between housings. It can be self-cooled or force-cooled with circulating gas or liquid. One common enclosure without barriers is nonsegregated; with metal barriers it's segregated; insulated cables in a common enclosure is cable bus. Source: IEEE C37.23-2015, clause 3 (types of metal-enclosed bus assemblies).
reference: IEEE C37.23-2015, clause 3 (types of metal-enclosed bus assemblies)

question: A bus run's phase conductors turn out to be insulated cables laid in a common metal enclosure with no barriers between phases. IEEE C37.23 calls this:
choices: Isolated-phase bus
Segregated-phase bus
Cable bus, which is built much like nonsegregated-phase bus
Not metal-enclosed bus at all
explanation: Cable bus is one of the four metal-enclosed bus types. It uses insulated cables as the main phase conductors, usually all in one enclosure without metal barriers, so in layout it resembles nonsegregated-phase bus. It can have one or several cables per phase depending on the current. Source: IEEE C37.23-2015, clause 3 (types of metal-enclosed bus assemblies).
reference: IEEE C37.23-2015, clause 3 (types of metal-enclosed bus assemblies)

question: Some metal-enclosed bus runs use transposition, where the three phase conductors swap positions along the length. What is it for?
choices: To give each phase the same inductive (proximity) effect from the other two
To make phasing tests unnecessary
To shorten the run
To let one phase be tested while the others stay energized
explanation: In a flat arrangement the middle conductor sits in a different magnetic environment from the outer ones. Swapping positions evenly along the run evens out the proximity effect each phase sees from the other two, which balances the phase impedances. You still phase-test tie sections from their permanent sources. Source: IEEE C37.23-2015, clause 3 (transposition); ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.4.B.5.

question: Inspecting segregated-phase bus, you compare the metal between phases with the covers. Per IEEE C37.23 construction rules:
choices: Phase barriers are heavier gauge (not less than MSG No. 11, about 3 mm) than covers and panels (not less than MSG No. 14, about 1.9 mm)
Phase barriers may be any insulating board
Barriers and covers are the same gauge
Covers are heavier than barriers because they face the room
explanation: C37.23 sets a minimum of MSG No. 14 (nominal 1.9 mm) for covers, barriers, and panels in general, and a heavier MSG No. 11 (nominal 3 mm) for the metal barriers between phases of segregated-phase bus. A thin or missing phase barrier on segregated bus is a construction finding, not a cosmetic one. Source: IEEE C37.23-2015, 7.1.1.
